episode_title: Your Process Has One Lane But Your Work Doesn't

real_qa.q: Why does a growing backlog or queue often look like a capacity problem when the real issue is process structure?
real_qa.r: A backlog that appears to be a capacity problem often stems from having one static process trying to carry multiple different types of workflow. In the example given, a client with a 40-line backlog thought they needed to add another person, but the real issue was that they had one FIFO process handling three different workflow types. Simple items were stuck behind complex projects that required additional work, creating the illusion of insufficient capacity when the problem was actually process design.
real_qa.requete: backlog looks like capacity problem process

real_qa.q: What is the express lane solution for managing mixed-complexity work in order entry and estimating?
real_qa.r: The express lane approach involves working the estimating backlog from both ends rather than strict FIFO. The strategy surfaces less complex items to get them moving quickly while simultaneously spending the required time on complex projects. This approach allows customers requesting simple quotes or quick answers to be served efficiently without waiting behind complex jobs, while the team still dedicates adequate attention to complex work that requires it.
real_qa.requete: express lane order entry backlog FIFO

real_qa.q: How did relocating a facility and onboarding an entirely new customer service team create a backlog crisis?
real_qa.r: When a facility had to relocate and hire, onboard, and train an entire new customer service team unfamiliar with the business, products, and services, the estimating backlog, order entry backlog, and all customer inquiries continued to pile up. Every time progress was made, something complex would derail the entire system. The team kept fighting the problem uphill because complex work would interrupt progress, and they could never get ahead because work was being processed in strict FIFO order regardless of complexity.

real_qa.q: What is the batching effect trap in custom manufacturing and service-based businesses?
real_qa.r: The batching effect occurs when businesses group similar work to reduce setup time or routing overhead, causing them to delay simple jobs that are due soon in order to batch them together. In manufacturing, this might mean running two jobs two weeks from now that are also due two weeks from now just to save a setup, while meanwhile three simpler jobs are shipping late today. In service businesses, this manifests as routing all inbound tickets together rather than handling simple ones immediately.

real_qa.q: When should an express lane or hybrid model be created versus temporary overtime or backlog shuffling?
real_qa.r: An express lane makes sense when the pattern repeats regularly and the business genuinely has different types of work at different complexity levels that flow predictably. If backlog buildup is rare and unpredictable, temporary solutions like overtime or a one-time backlog shuffle may make more sense. Cross-training is almost always valuable, but creating a permanent express lane should be tied to understanding whether this is a recurring business pattern or an anomaly.
